GIS and retirement withdrawals: why RRSP and TFSA cash can land in different income years

Four charts separate RRSP income inclusion, the TFSA benefit exemption, official 2026 GIS maximums by household status, and the usual July review calendar.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

CRA says an RRSP withdrawal is included in income for the year withdrawn; CRA says TFSA income and withdrawals do not affect federal income-tested benefits, including GIS. The central idea

A withdrawal can be spendable cash now and affect a later income-tested benefit review. Trace the registered-account source and tax year first, then confirm the amount with Service Canada.

01

Start with the account source, not only the cash target

Suppose a retired person wants CAD 12,000 for a one-time expense. A withdrawal from a regular RRSP is generally included in income in the calendar year it is withdrawn. Tax may be withheld at the source, but the withheld amount is a prepayment; the final tax depends on the return. The RRSP withdrawal rule is confirmed in CRA Guide T4040.

A TFSA can supply the same gross CAD 12,000 without affecting federal income-tested benefits such as the Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS). CRA says both income earned in a TFSA and amounts withdrawn from it do not affect eligibility for those federal benefits. This does not mean every retirement-income comparison favours a TFSA: the accounts have different contribution and tax histories, and the source of a withdrawal does not settle its overall tax cost or suitability.

The chart deliberately compares a stated RRSP income addition with the published TFSA benefit treatment. It is not a dollar-for-dollar estimate of GIS lost. Other income, eligible deductions, relationship status and the rules used in the actual benefit calculation remain relevant. Use the source distinction to ask a better question, not to substitute a shortcut for the Service Canada calculation.

02

Map the income year to the later GIS review

Service Canada reviews GIS each year using the federal tax return. It says the July letter will confirm whether the benefit is renewed, stopped, resumed or needs more income information. In the ordinary prior-year example, an RRSP withdrawal during 2025 appears on the 2025 return and is relevant to the July 2026 review period, which runs July 2026 through June 2027. The withdrawal date within 2025 changes how long the calendar interval feels, but does not move it into a separate monthly tax year.

Payment amounts are adjusted in January, April, July and October when the cost of living rises. A single quarterly maximum therefore should not be multiplied by twelve and presented as a guaranteed annual payment. The interactive calendar counts the month-start intervals from a selected withdrawal month to the next ordinary July review; it does not promise when an application or adjustment will be processed.

There is an important current-income route. If you or your spouse or common-law partner has lower annual income because of retirement, or other pension benefits are reduced or stopped, Service Canada says to contact it. It may set the benefit using estimated income for the current year instead of the previous year's income. Report material changes and confirm what documents or estimate it requires; the chart does not trigger a review.

03

Read the published maximums as dated reference points

The official amount page, updated 13 October 2026, shows an October–December 2026 table with a maximum GIS payment of CAD 1,138.90 per month for a single, divorced or widowed recipient and up to CAD 685.56 for someone whose spouse or common-law partner receives full OAS or the Allowance. It shows up to CAD 1,138.90 where the spouse receives neither OAS nor the Allowance. The companion annual income ceilings shown on the same page are CAD 23,112, CAD 30,528, CAD 42,768 and CAD 55,392 respectively; couple amounts use combined income.

These are official program figures, not sample household observations or guaranteed payments. The page says GIS depends on marital status and previous-year income and that actual payments may be lower. The chart preserves the four distinct relationship cases and their published denominators. It does not average them together or treat one person's threshold as a couple threshold. Use the current GIS amount information and estimator for a live case; confirm the applicable quarter and current records.

04

Build a small dated map before choosing a funding source

Write down the cash date, the source account, the calendar year in which the withdrawal is reportable, the tax return that records it and the benefit period that may use that return. Keep tax withheld on an RRSP payment in a separate column from final tax. If you have a spouse or common-law partner, note the combined-income treatment and any change in marital status. Then compare an RRSP draw with available TFSA or cash funding while accounting for contribution-room constraints, liquidity and the assets left for later years.

This tool uses one invented CAD 12,000 withdrawal and a selectable year and month. It shows the amount tied to each source rule and the ordinary July review calendar. It does not estimate tax, actual GIS, eligibility, couple income, TFSA contribution room, portfolio return, other benefits or an optimal withdrawal order. Its maximum-payment reference is fixed to October–December 2026 and is not a forecast for later quarters. Verify a real payment with Service Canada and CRA records before relying on the result.
